certainty_reasoning: Both men's own letters survive and both are quoted here, which is the README's self-reported test met from both sides. Stafford's letter of May 1877 asks Whitman to 'take me back and love me the same' and signs itself 'Your lovin but bad tempered Harry'; Whitman's letters run from 'Dear Hank' to 'Your Walt', and his notebooks call Stafford 'the central figure of them all'. The Whitman Archive's own correspondent note states that the relationship 'also had a romantic, erotic charge to it'. What the record does not settle is how far that went, and the scholarship openly disagrees - Kantrowitz reports readings ranging 'from asexual and paternal to erotic and promiscuous', and Stafford's own line about 'something wanting to compleete our friendship' is glossed by Kantrowitz with a 'perhaps'. This entry records who attests the bond, not what they did.
date_label: met in 1876 at the Camden New Republic, Stafford eighteen and Whitman fifty-seven; closest through the Timber Creek years to about 1884, when Stafford married; the two remained in contact until Whitman's death in 1892
summary: Harry Stafford was an errand boy of eighteen when Whitman met him in a Camden newspaper office in 1876. He took the poet home to his parents' tenant farm at Kirkwood, where Whitman spent the next several summers bathing in Timber Creek and wrestling saplings back to health, and where the two shared a top-floor bedroom. It was a quarrelsome, unequal, much-interrupted attachment - Whitman gave Stafford a friendship ring and Stafford gave it back more than once - and it is the relationship early Whitman scholarship most successfully ignored, because Traubel's first six volumes never mention his name. Whitman's friend John Burroughs, less discreetly, complained that the two 'cut up like two boys'.

sources.quote: Dear Friend— You know how I left you at the station to-day. I have thought of it and cannot get it off my mind, so I have come up to ask your forgiveness. I know how I have served you on many occasions before. I know that it is my falt and not yours. Can you forgive me and take me back and love me the same I will try by the grace of God to do better. I cannot give you up, and it makes me feel so bad to think how we have spent the last day or two; and all for my temper. … Cant you take me back and love me the same. Your lovin but bad tempered Harry.
sources.context: Stafford to Whitman, dated by Miller to 1 May 1877, after a quarrel at the station. Stafford was eighteen. The elision drops one sentence about his temper sending him to prison. **The spelling is Stafford's** - 'falt', 'Cant', 'lovin' - and the archive flags each instance in its markup. The letter is written on the back of someone else's letter to Whitman, which is its own small fact about who had paper. This is the fullest surviving statement from Stafford's side.
sources.supports: The younger participant's own words - the asking-back, the 'I cannot give you up', and the register of the whole attachment.

sources.quote: Dear Hank— Yours of 9th rec'd—am a little surprised you take to L of G so quickly—I guess it is because the last five years had been preparing & fixing the ground, more & more & more—& now that the seed is dropt in it sprouts quickly … Hank, I am still feeling under the weather—My appetite is fair, (when I can get what I like)—& sleep middling, but I am as weak as a cat … (Hank, you do not appreciate your mother—there is not a nobler woman in Jersey)— Your Walt
sources.context: Whitman to Stafford, 11 February 1881, from Camden, five years into the acquaintance; the envelope is addressed to 'Harry Lamb Stafford | Kirkwood | Glendale | New Jersey'. Whitman had given him a copy of Leaves of Grass four days earlier. The register is the ordinary one of this correspondence - domestic, instructive, unguarded about his own body - and it is worth recording precisely because it is not ardent: the attachment ran mostly at this temperature.
sources.supports: The sustained private correspondence and its everyday register.

sources.quote: Stafford and Whitman slept together in the same top floor bedroom, and when they traveled together Whitman referred to him as "my nephew" and insisted that they be accommodated in the same bed. … Despite the frolicking, the relationship was a stormy one. They quarreled frequently, and several times Stafford returned a friendship ring given to him by Whitman. … The nature of their bond remains mysterious, and critics have interpreted it as everything from asexual and paternal to erotic and promiscuous.
sources.context: Arnie Kantrowitz's reference entry on Stafford. Recorded as the second-hand layer, and kept at length because its last sentence is the honest state of the scholarship. The elisions drop Burroughs's complaint that the two 'cut up like two boys' and Stafford's own 'something wanting to compleete [sic] our friendship', which Kantrowitz glosses 'perhaps meaning sexual relations'. Kantrowitz also records that Whitman met a Stafford farm hand, Ed Cattell, at the creek and kept those meetings secret from Stafford - see cattell--whitman.
sources.supports: The shared bed, the ring, the quarrels - and that the sexual question is contested among specialists rather than settled.

null_findings.finding: DATE CONFLICT, unresolved and left standing. Stafford's marriage to Eva Westcott is given as **1884** by Kantrowitz's encyclopedia entry and as **1883** by the correspondent note the Whitman Archive attaches to Stafford's letters - two statements on the same site. Neither is followed here; the bio and date_label carry both. ALSO NOTED, as a caution for any older secondary source on Whitman's circle: the archive states Stafford's name appears **nowhere in the first six volumes** of Traubel's With Walt Whitman in Camden, and only in the last three, published in the 1990s. An absence in Traubel is not evidence of absence in Whitman's life.
